MILLER (South Grey) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 73) to amend the Interest Act. He said: I introduced a Bill in the earlier part of the session having the same object as that

which I seek to accomplish by this measure. Some question was raised as to whether we had jurisdiction, and I withdrew that Bill and introduced another, the one now before the House, to which, I am sure, no such objection can be made. This Bill provides, in effect, that a mortgagor may repay overdue principal on a mortgage at any time by giving one month's notice, or by the payment of one month's interest by way of bonus in lieu of notice. I think that this is a perfectly fair provision and one that no mortgagee or other person can reasonably take any objection to.	The Bill as I have introduced it is not retroactive. It provides, however, that though the terms of the contract of mortgage may stipulate that overdue principal cannot be repaid except upon payment of a bonus, yet, notwithstanding that, the mortgagor may pay on giving one month's notice or by paying one month's interest by way of bonus. Now, principal on a mortgage can only remain past due, the mortgage can only be permitted to remain in arrears, bv the consent or action of both parties, the borrower and the lender. And, if both parties agree to allow a mortgage to remain in arrears, I think their rights ought to be as nearly as possible equal. What are the rights of the mortgagee? He has the right to take action against the mortgagor to recover payment of his principal without notice at all. Usually, he has power to sell under the mortgage on giving one month's notice. However, most of our loan companies in the province of Ontario-and I think in the western provinces as well-say that if the principal remains overdue for a certain longer period of time the right of sale may be exercised without notice at all. The mortgagee may take foreclosure proceedings without notice. He may bring suit, without notice, for the recovery of past-due principal under the covenants of the mortgagor to pay. The mortgagee, having power to call in his overdue principal without notice, ought to extend the samS privilege of repaying overdue principal without notice. I am not asking to go as far in favour of the mortgagor as that, but only that he may be permitted to pay on one month's notice. In the province of Ontario we have a law of the legislature permitting the mortgagor to repay overdue principal on giving three months' notice or on a payment of three months' interest by way of bonus. I seek to shorten that time to one month. Private parties lending money on mortgage in Ontario do not exact the three months' notice or three months' interest by way of bonus. It is, however, the common practice of the loan companies. I may be told that in this Bill I seek to interfere with the contracts of parties and
that we ought not to interfere with contracts which parties have chosen to enter into. I say, in reply to that, that a great deal of our legislation does interfere with contracts between parties. Besides, I would point out the manner in which the contract is usually entered into by the mortgagor. He applies for a loan. He usually wants the money at a certain date; he wants to pay off a mortgage, to buy property, or to meet a maturing liability. There is not usually the condition in the application that he would have to pay three months' interest or give three months' notice in repaying overdue principal; he does not discover that condition until he comes to sign the mortgage a few days before he is to use the money. The mortgage form usually used by loan companies is a long form containing many covenants. It would take a long time for a mortgagor to read his mortgage, and the chances are only one in a hundred that he would understand the contract even if he took the pains to read it over. But suppose that if he did read and understand the contract, yet if he refused to execute it would mean delay in getting the money of which, perhaps, he is urgently in need at the time. And he would probably be told, if he refused to sign because of that clause that he would have to pay the expenses of the inspection of his property and of the solicitor in preparing the mortgage as well as the commission to the agent to obtain the loan. So, to avoid expense and delay, and as the misfortune-if it turns out to be one-is five years in the future, he usually signs the mortgage. In reply to this contention that I am interfering in contracts between parties, I would point out that we have on our statute-book a law, introduced by Hon. Edward Blake in 1880, now and for thirty years the law of Canada, that, if the mortgagor borrows money it may be upon mortgage for twenty, fifteen or ten years, yet, notwith standing that he has contracted to use the money and pay interest for that length of time, after he has used the money for five years, he may repay it by. giving three months' interest by wav of bonus. So, we have the example of interfering with contracts in-exactly the same way. As matters are to-day, a man borrows money: When the principal becomes due, the loan company, if they cannot at the time lend the money in some other place at better advantage, allow the mortgage to remain in arrears until they can call it in and lend the money at a higher rate of interest. Then, at a time when it will be of great disadvantage to the mortgagor, the money is called in to be lent at a higher rate, and the mortgagor, of course, must renew t the higher rate, or get the money from some one else. Now if this Bill becomes law,

the practice then will be that mortgagee loan companies will attend promptly to the renewal of their loans as they become due, and then the mortgagor and the mortgagee will have equal chances, whether the rates of interest go up or go down.
When I introduced the first Bill it was objected to on the ground of lack of jurisdiction, and in order to get over that objection I have used in the Bill I am now discussing the exact language of the Hon. Edward Blake, and it is found in section 10, chapter 120 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906. In the Bill I first introduced I said that the mortgagor might pay off the mortgage upon giving one month's notice of payment, or upon paying one month's interest. But in this Bill I say, as Mr. Blake said in his section, that upon the payment, or upon the tender oi principle money with one month's additional interest, or one month's notice, if it be refused, thereafter no interest shall be collected, which is in effect saying that the mortgagor may repay and the mortgagee must accept. But the wording I have used brings the Bill clearly within the jurisdiction of this House, as I am sure the Minister of Justice will say, because under clause 19 of section 91 of the British North America Act, we in this House have the right to deal with the question of interest. I have talked to many members of the House, some of whom are not here to-night, and I met with scarcely any one who has any objection to the Bill, and most of them are warmly in favour of it. Therefore I trust it may receive the support of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When my hon. friend moved the second reading of the Bill for which the present one is substituted, a good deal of objection seemed to be offered by several members of the House to the proposition, and a grave question was raised by eminent legal gentlemen as to the right of this House to legislate upon such a subject. It was urged that what was really being done by the Bill then under consideration, was to make a new contract for the lender and borrower, and to substitute that new statutory contract for the one which, by the instrument of mortgage, they had entered into. I think there was considerable doubt on the phraseology used in that Bill, whether what was legislated about did fall within the subject of interest, in regard to which of course this parliament has, under the British North America Act, the exclusive right to legislate. No doubt my hon. friend was so advised, because he withdrew that measure, with the leave of the House, and has substituted this one for it. Now, so far as the wording of the present Bill is concerned, I think every one will be compelled to agree that it legislates only with respect Mr. MILLER.
to interest, and therefore it would be competent for this parliament to pass the legislation in question, if it was thought right to do so. But while that is probably the case, I think we cannot close our eyes to the fact that the effect of this legislation, if it becomes law, will be to substitute a new contract made in virtue of this Act of parliament, for the contract which the lender and borrower have entered into at the time the money was loaned; and then the question is whether the House is prepared to take that step; or, having the power to do it, whether it is expedient to exercise that power. Now, I quite agree that time was when, under the hardships of usurious contracts, gross impositions were practised upon needy borrowers at the hands of greedy lenders. I doubt if that time is still with us. I think we have come to such a state of things in this country, perhaps in all civilized countries, that at this date money is simply a commodity, and the man who has it charges for its use just what it will bring in the money markets of the world. The man who needs it knows that he is not in any way restricted to one lender. If he cannot get what he wants upon the security which he has to offer in one quarter, he will go to another. No doubt, just to the extent to which the security which he has may be poor, just to that extent he will have to pay a higher price for the accommodation which he desires in the shape of a larger rate of interest. I think it would not be wise to try to control freedom of contract as to the amount of interest, iat any rate an amount within reason, which a borrower who requires to use money for a little time, is willing to pay and contracts to pay to the lender. Now, it seems to me that this is a proposition practically of a similar character to a proposition to regulate the rate of interest which a borrower should pay or which a lender .should take. It does not seem to me that it is anything unconscionable for a lender to stipulate, when advancing his money to the borrower, that if it is not paid when it is due, he shall have three months' notice before being compelled to take it. I think experience shows that an investor who lives by lending to others the money which' his labour, it may be, has accumulated, finds that he cannot secure a new investment, upon the average, in less than three months' time. He may be fortunate in being able to lend his money almost immediately after it is paid, but he is quite as likely, it seems to me, to have to wait longer than three months before he finds a new investment for that money as to find one within less than that time. But, however that may be, if he says to .the borrower openly and fairly when negotiating their contract of repayment:	Now if you
cannot pay me, if you do not pay me on the day that you agree to pay, if you let it

run any _ longer, you must give me three months' interest, or the equivalent of three; months' interest, in lieu of the notice; and if the borrower says, I am quite content, and makes that contract with his eyes open, I do not see why parliament should step in and say: No, we won't allow that bargain to have its course, we force you, Mr. Lender, to take one month's interest, or one month's notice, upon penalty that if you do not do it, you shall get no more interest at all.
That is exactly the substance of my hon. friend's proposition. He says that if the money is not paid when it is due, then, notwithstanding any agreement that the parties may have made between them, if the borrower gives at any time thereafter one month's notice to the lender that he is willing to pay at the expiration of the month, then, if the lender will not take payment, he forfeits all further interest. It is a question whether the House is prepared to interfere to that extent with the freedom of contract that ought to obtain, and which it is in the general interest should obtain between men in ordinary business transactions. For myself, I should doubt very much the advisability of doing it. It seems to me it is going to make money harder to get on the part of the borrower. It seems to me that when the lender sees before him this provision of the law he will say to the borrower: I will not let you have the money at all, or if I let you have it, I will charge you a higher rate of interest, say one half per cent, or something of the sort, by reason of the fact that I shall forfeit all interest unless I take my money at a month's notice. It would strike me that it would be better to leave things to the play of actual business conditions and competition between lenders who are anxious to find places where they can make their money earn interest, and bring them in a return. I am quite aware that we have at present upon our statute-book a provision which my hon. friend has adapted and followed very closely in the framing of this clause. In our present Interest Act there is a provision applicable to mortgages of Teal estate which have five years and more to run, that whenever any principal money or interest secured by such an instrument is not payable for more than five years after the date of the mortgage, then, if at any time after the expiration of that period, any person liable to pay tenders or pays to the person entitled to receive the money the amount of principal and interest to the time of payment, together with three months' further interest, no further interest shall be chargeable.

I would like to ask the Minister of Justice whether or not the section he has just referred to is not in effect a
much greater interference with contracts between parties than the Bill which I am discussing and which I have introduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Very possibly it is, but that is not the point. I am saying that I am quite aware that this section is on our statute-books. It gives the lender three months interest or three months notice. My hon. friend proposes to reduce that to one month and to extend his legislation to all mortgages, whereas the present enactment is limited to mortgages of real estate. But whether or not the present provision of the law is a greater interference with the freedom of contract, I was intending to point out something as to the circumstances under which that provision of the law found its place in the statute-book, as it seemed to me to illustrate the inadvisability of putting anything else upon the same line on our statute-book. That provision of the law was introduced nearly thirty years ago, in the session of 1880, and, referring to the debate upon the subject at that time, it appears that the Bill, introduced by a private member, a supporter of the government of the day, was opposed apparently by every single member of the government. It met with strong objection, with a great deal of opposition and criticism just upon the ground that I have indicated, because it was considered an unwarrantable interference with the freedom and sacredness of a contract solemnly entered into. It was passed, however, notwithstanding the opposition of the members of the government in a body over their votes. It has been law ever since. I do not know what influence it may have had in the framing of contracts since that date, but I think it is very probable that the presence of that enactment upon our law books has been the reason for the very general term of three months' notice or three months' bonus which is to be found to-day in most of the mortgages that are current. Parties have contracted to correspond with that provision of the law, and parties having so contracted, if you are now going to say in regard to future contracts that the time has to be shortened in the interests of the borrower and against the interests of the lender, it seems to me that the result can scarcely fail to be what I have tried to point out.
Let me just say one other thing. I think the conditions were to a marked degree different in 1880 in respect to the ease or difficulty with which money could be borrowed from what they are in the year 1910. At any rate in the part of the country from which I come I know that in those years one great evil which every borrower felt and which was very widespread was the habit which lending companies or building I societies had of disguising the true rate of

interest they were exacting from their borrowers by the manner in which they framed their mortgages. Their mortgages calculated the interest along with the principal for the full period the mortgage was to run; then adding the total amount of the interest to the principal, they were in the habit of dividing it up into as many payments as the borrower desired, four per annum, perhaps, and, so dividing it up, they took from the borrower each quarter, from the time that he borrowed the money until he had paid the whole of that money, except the last instalment, the same amount; so that a man, after he had practically paid off the whole, or the greater part of his principal, was in reality paying perhaps fourteen, fifteen, or eighteen per cent, instead of the six, or seven, or eight per cent that, he thought he was agreeing to pay, and which upon computation he would appear to be paying. That was an evil and this legislation cured it. There are no more of such mortgages. Now, a man borrows money, whether from a private individual or a company, upon plain straight payments of simple interest calculated at a fixed per cent and payable either annually or semi-annually. If a man, entering into a contract for repayment with his eyes open and in perfect freedom, agrees that he will pay three months' interest in case he is not able to pay at maturity, or give three months' notice, it does not seem' that such- :a man needs the protection of legislation to change his contract and where there is no great evil to be met by the legislation my hon. friend is proposing, it would seem to me to be contrary to good policy to pass it.

When this question was up earlier in the session I took strong ground that the proposition then made by my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) was ultra vires of this parliament, but I am satisfied that the present Bill is intra vires. That is admitted by the Minister of Justice, and I presume it will not be controverted by any member of the House. It, therefore, becomes a question of policy whether this Bill shall become law or not. And, while I am very diffident in dissenting from the judgment of so mature a mind as that of the Minister of Justice, yet, when it is a question not of law but of policy every member of the House has a right to exercise his judgment. The Minister of Justice has advanced somewhat strong reasons against the passage of the Bill, but there are reasons equally strong on the other side and which I think outweigh those given by my hon. friend. The Minister of Justice puts forward the proposition that this is a contract and that we have no right to interfere with it. I admit that if it be purely a question of contract between two parties this parliament has perhaps no right to interfere, although every session Mr. AYLESWORTH.
of parliament since I have been here we have passed legislation which has interfered with contracts. The lending of money has become so muih concentrated in the hands of loan companies in Canada that it is almost a necessity to go to these companies to obtain a loan. They have become practically a public utility, and if the loan companies make unreasonable contracts I see no reason why they should not be curtailed the same as unreasonable contracts made by public utility companies. For instance, within the last year or two the Railway Commission has found it necessary to interfere with contracts made by railway companies and the shippers of goods all over the country. The shipper was compelled to sign an application on the back of which were laid down conditions which for the most part never were read, and which the ordinary man could not understand the legal significance of, and as a result of that contract if the goods were lost or damaged in transit the shipper had no redress against the railway company. These contracts have been interfered with and modified by the Railway Commission. In the same way when one sends a telegram he has to accept a certain contract, and I venture to say that not one member out of 50 in this House has ever read the terms of it. When we go to these public companies they compel us to accept contracts, the true intent of which most people do not realize, and to a very great extent it is the same with a loan company. I may be prejudiced against loan companies. When I first Commenced practising law I was looking after all the dollars I could earn, and I accepted the solicitorship of a loan company, but I resigned after a year because in my judgment its proceeding was the most unfair proposition I ever was called upon to sanction. I will not mention any name, but that loan company compelled the borrower to sign a contract and give a mortgage along the lines of equal payments. I admit that a great majority of loan companies at present, or possibly all of them have abolished that form of contract. It was a most unfair contract and the borrower was compelled to sign conditions without knowing their true legal import. The Minister of Justice says it is not fair that a man who has made a contract that he shall not be compelled to take his money without receiving an advance of three months' interest should be compelled to receive an advance of one month's interest. I would like to know wherein a loan company differs from a bank. The loan company lends its money to the public on long terms and the bank lends on short term loans. But what would you think of a bank which would say that because the borrower did not pay his note yesterday when it was due he would have to pay a month's interest in advance be-

fore being allowed to redeem it. A cry would go up against such a stipulation which would soon be heard in this parliament. You know, Sir, the hardest thing in this world is to take from the privileged classes privileges which they have enjoyed in the past. We meet it every day; they are meeting it now in the old country, but from time to time these privileges are curtailed and no great damage is done, and the only wonder expressed is that they were not curtailed long before. If this Bill becomes law now I have no doubt that a year hence people will wonder why such legislation was not passed years before. I do not think a loan company or any one else suffers if a reasonable advance is given when money was not paid on-the very day it was due. I do not know whether any members in this House have had experience in trying to get these loan companies to release a mortgage before it became due. It will be found that in many cases where a man may have an opportunity to dispose of a part or the whole of his property, he cannot do it until the mortgage is taken off, and some of these loan companies in order to relieve the property will ask not one month's interest or three months' interest, but I have never known a case where they took less than six months' interest, and I know numbers of cases where they wanted a year's interest. I do not think the loan companies are entitled to very much pity from this parliament if the Bill should pass. I believe in evenhanded justice and in treating them fairly, but if ever there was a measure advanced in this House which appeals to my sense of justice and fair play it is the Bill we are now considering and I shall have much pleasure in voting for it.

Before making some very brief remarks on this Bill I wish to premise by giving my interpretation of it, which, I think, does not conflict with that of the Minister of Justice, although it possibly does with that of the hon. member (Mr. Carvell). It does not appear to me that there is any retroactive feature in the Bill. The first sentence strictly confines the operation of the Act to such contracts as are hereinafter entered into. I do not think the placing of the comma in the third line before the word ' after ' instead of after the word ' Act ' has any other effect. If I thought it had any other effect, and if I thought it had in particular the effect of making this Bill retroactive I could not support that feature of it. Therefore, premising that the Bill can only operate as regards mortgages or renewals of mortgages entered into after the passing of the Act, I wish to state to the House my reasons for supporting it. It seems to me that the principal that should govern this House with regard to all these Bills is that we
should ask ourselves whether or not the legislation is in the public interest. If it is in the public interest, then it seems to me this House is justified even to the extent of breaking into contracts Already existing. It would, of course,' in such instances, take much more to convince this House that such a Bill would be in the public interest, but that is all that should in the ultimate determine any member in his choice. How far does the Bill go? It says that once a mortgage falls due, and is not paid, thereafter, unless the mortgage company or mortgagee says to the mortgagor: Come out into the open daylight, sign a new contract knowing its terms, they must accept the money on one month's notice. If the mortgagor is not in a position to pay, he is subject to the remedies of the mortgage and the mortgagee call insist on those remedies or make it uncomfortable for. the mortgagor. If the' mortgagor does not pay at the time the payment falls due, the mortgagee is compelled to go to him and explain the facts to him and say: Unless you are ready to pay, you must enter into a new contract. If the mortgagee lies silent, site by and lets things run, he has to take the consequence and has to say: I must take my money on one month's notice. There is no hardship there; what is the benefit? It strikes me there is a very considerable benefit. In the first place the Minister of Justice argues that conditions now differ very materially from those that obtained years ago when the Act introduced by the Hon. Edward Blake to which he referred was passed. It may be that in Ontario, and particularly within the clientage to which the Minister of Justice was in some degree confined, such conditions have changed, but out in western Canada I do not think I am going beyond the mark in saying that the conditions referred to by him, as existing at that time exist now in even a more marked degree. The average mortgagee throughout the newer parts of western Canada is no more on a par with the mortgagee, and particularly with a mortgage company than the average mortgagor was at the time of the introduction of the legislation referred to by the Minister of Justice with the mortgagee of that day. In a very great number of cases the mortgagor in those parts of the country is now a foreigner. I doubt not but in four cases out of seven the man who signs a mortgage on his land in western Canada has no real appreciation whatever of most of the clauses of the mortgage, and it is impossible for him to form an intelligent idea particularly of the penal clauses of the mortgage. Consequently it is not only within the power but I think it is the duty of this House, where-ever it can with advantage, to step in between these parties and make it impossible for an unfair contract to be perpetrated. The Minister of Justice has stated that we

should not stand between the mortgagor and the mortgagee and say to them: You must not enter into a contract whereby you shall penalize a mortgagor and .compel him to give three months' or six months' notice in case, on the very day the mortgage is due, he finds he has not paid it or is not able to pay it. I do not see that any great injustice can .be done by this. So long as all the remedies exercisable under that mortgage are still allowed the mortgagee, there can be no injustice to him, and at the same time we say that if the mortgagor, who is generally not on a par with the mortgagee, runs over the time he can pay it off on one month's notice unless the mortgagee informs him of all the facts on the day it falls due or shortly after and says: Come and enter into a new agreement. There is no hardship on the mortgagee that I can see. I do not think this House is likely to go too far in protecting the mortgagor. The different provinces have invaded the very field which the Minister of Justice holds so sacred. Throughout Canada, at all events in the province from which I come, recent legislation was passed affecting the relations between lender and borrower, and I must say that that legislation has worked out very favourably in the public interest. To-day in Manitoba any contract whereby the borrower undertakes To pay a greater rate of interest than 12 per cent is declared usurious, penalties are imposed on the lender, and he is unable to collect. That is the field the Minister of Justice holds sacred from invasion. This legislation is along the same lines as the legislation quoted by the Minister of Justice which certainly has been in the public interest, and when the minister acknowledges that in his long experience he has not seen any detrimental effect from that legislation, it seems to me that acknowledgment should go a long way to establish in our minds that no such detrimental effect has ensued. Surely the legislation referred to was in the public interest, but would it be in the public interest to-day to permit mortgage companies to tie up properties for 20 or 40 years, to make it impossible to give clear titles to property for great length of time? The legislation has been taken advantage of on many occasions and very properly, and with good effect. This is along the same lines, a step in the right direction. It does not go very far; I would like to see it go further to the extent of compelling mortgage companies either to take instalments as they fall due or to take payment on one month's notice. If it went to that extent it would seem to me more advantageous than it is, but going to the extent it does, I think it will work for the general advantage of the people and that it should receive my vote.

Mr. Speaker, I can only say that I am going to support the Bill as it is. As it was before, it was retroactive and, as I told the mover, I could not support it for that reason. I do not think it will work any particular hardship; on the contrary a good many mortgage companies and trust companies do not put those clauses in their mortgages. I know that many mortgagors do not read mortgages carefully enough. The difficulty is that they trust to the people from whom they are getting the money to a very large extent, and they do not read the mortgages through at all, but just the amounts and the interest. I do not think it will work any hardship, because lenders Will accommodate themselves to this law after it is passed. As my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has stated very clearly, when the mortgage is due, if they cannot pay it, it is the lender's option then to make them renew the debt so that he can protect himself in that way. So far as I am personally concerned- and I have a good deal to do with lending money-I have never in ten years asked a mortgagor to sign a mortgage which had a penalty clause of that kind in it, without thoroughly explaining it, and when I explain it, the mortgagor will not sign. There is too much competition for the lending of money now, and consequently, in my section of the country at least, no need for borrowers to sign contracts containing any such clause. If a loan or trust company will not loan to the individual without such a penalty, the borrower can easily get the money from some one else. So far as the people I represent are concerned, they would be satisfied with the Bill as it is, and for that reason I shall certainly support it.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice says we have no right to interfere with contracts entered into by people with their eyes open and with perfect freedom. I have tried to point out that these contracts are not entered into openly and freely. In 99 cases out of 100 the mortgagors are entirely ignorant that the contract signed contains any such provision. The hon. minister fears that one effect of the passing of this legislation will be to make it harder to borrow money on mortgage and raise the rate of interest. Well, I do not think we need apprehend any danger on that score because there is too much competition in the lending of money. The loan companies are the only ones that insert such a clause as I object to. It is not inserted by the trust companies, the life insurance companies and private lenders, so that there is no danger of any increase in the rates of interest. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice says that we have no

right to interfere with contracts, and he pointed out that the hon. gentleman who introduced section 10 of the Interest Act, which enables a man to pay off a mortgage any time after five years, no matter how long he may have contracted to keep the mortgage alive, was introduced by a private member and carried against the votes of members of the government. But the private member who introduced that Bill, which is still in our statutes, was the Hon. Edward Blake. He introduced it thirty years ago, and it has been the law ever since, and most excellent law it has proved. And although that law was passed in opposition to the votes of gentlemen then composing the government, if any government wanted to repeal that section 10, there would be a row that would cause them a good deal of trouble. If that law be right, then there is no reason why we should not pass the legislation I am submitting. What is the difference between section 10 introduced by Mr. Blake and section 10a of the same Act which I am submitting? Under Mr. Blake's amendment, although a man may have borrowed money for a term of twenty years and agreed to keep paying the interest during that term, and not pay off the capital, he was given the privilege of paying off his debt at the end of five years in spite of his agreement, and thus getting rid of the mortgage. Compare that with the amendment I propose. By my amendment, section 10a, I provide that if the money borrowed be not paid at the time stipulated, the mortgagor may give one month's notice of his intention to pay or pay one month's interest as a bonus, and the creditor is obliged to accept the same.. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Portage La Prairie (Mr. Meighen) this is not interfering with an existing contract at all, but simply provides that certain contracts should not be entered into in the future because they are contrary to public interests. We are passing similar legislation from year to year both in the provincial legislatures and this parliament. In Ontario, and no doubt in the other provinces, we have the Mechanics' Lien Act, which provides that although a mechanic enters into a contract to waive his rights to a lien for the work he has done, that contract is void and null because contrary to public interest. In our Act regarding the water carriage of goods, introduced as a government measure this session, it is provided that although shippers may enter into certain contracts and sign certain bills of lading, they shall not be bound by the same. If, as we have been told to-night by the Minister of Justice, section 10 of the Interest Act was introduced 30 years ago by Mr. Blake, then a private member, contrary to the wishes and passed contrary to the votes of the then members of the government
My hon. friend is doing an injustice to another by saying that legislation was introduced by Mr. Blake. My recollection is that it was introduced by Dr. Orton.

Possibly, but it was fathered by Mr. Blake and is commonly called the Blake Act. If that Act, which was introduced and passed against the wishes of the government, has produced excellent results, it is a very good precedent, and I have no doubt that should the Bill I propose become law, excellent results will likewise follow.
Is there anything in it to apply to mortgages now existing or renewed or does it apply only to those hereafter created?
I have no wish to makd the Bill retroactive. It will only apply to mortgages hereafter made or renewed.
Better express that more clearly.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and House went into committee thereon.

I would call the attention of the mover of this Bill to this point: What would be the effect of it where there is no agreement at all? It seems to me that the courts would interpret the section to mean that if a man failed to pay his mortgage on the very day it was due he could not redeem it at all without giving a month's notice or paying a month's interest. Surely that cannot be the intention of my hon. friend (Mr. Miller). The section ought to be amended to make it clear that it is intended to apply only to cases where there is an agreement in the mortgage preventing the mortgagor repaying overdue principal without paying three months' interest or giving three months' notice. In the province from which I come a man is entitled, ordinarily, to pay his mortgage at any time after it becomes due, unless it runs on year after year with interest paid on it, in which case the courts hold, that an implied agreement has arisen between the parties which would prevent the money being paid off except upon notice, in some cases of three months, in some cases of six months according to the periods when the interest is payable. But, under this section, as I have said, it seems to me the courts would hold, in the absence of an agreement, that the mortgagor could not pay off except by giving a month's notice or paying a month's interest.
If the mortgagor does not pay when the mortgage is due, the company can exact the interest for a further term, and they do exact it.

But suppose there is no agreement about three months' notice or

interest, yet the mortgagor neglects to pay the mortgage when due, leaving it to run for a week. Then, under this section he qould not redeem ^except :on paying a month's interest. That is a hardship, and I do not think it is the intention of the mover of the Bill to make that the law.
Could not the object be accomplished by inserting another subsection, providing that section 10a shall not apply to any mortgage in which there is no agreement requiring three month's notice?

Another question which strikes me is whether the section, as framed, would really cover a case where there is a contract. Would not the courts hold that, as the section says nothing about a contract, parliament did not intend to cover a case where there was a contract between the narties? In that case, the section would be barren of results in che direction the hon. member (Mr. Miller) has in view. I may be wrong, but that is the view that presents itself to my mind at this time.

I cannot take that view. The whole tenor of the section is that, in any case, if the money be not paid when it is due, then, by tendering a month's interest or by giving a month's notice, the payment may be made. It seems to me that would be the case whether there was a contract requiring three months' notice or not. I am inclined to think the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) is right in his suggestion that this would apply to contracts where there was no penalty as well as to contracts in which there was a penalty.

As to the first suggestion, with all due deference-for I know the opinion of the Minister of Public Works in a matter of law would be accepted before mine-it seems to me that that hon. gentleman is right and that the courts would be very likely to hold this clause to imply necessarily that notice would be required under all conditions. As to the suggestion that it is doubtful that the courts would hold the section to apply as against express stipulation, I cannot say that I have the same view as the minister. In any case, I think both these points are capable of remedy, and I would suggest the following: -After the word ' then ' in the sixth line of the section, add the following words:
Notwithstanding any stipulation to the contrary in such mortgage or renewal.
That would cover it.

Then, to meet the other objection add the clause:
Provided nothing herein contained shall be held to require the giving of notice or paying of interest by the mortgagor which he is not Mr. PUGSLEY.
required to give or pay at the time of the passing of this Act.

Or it might be:
Where he is not required bv the mortgage or any agreement in respect thereto to give.
It requires careful drafting.

I think it would be as well for the committee to rise and report progress, and we will consider the Bill at another meeting.
Progress reported.
